claim: Animals use memory-guided and memory-independent strategies to make navigational decisions.
source: Animals use memory-guided and memory-independent strategies to make navigational decisions.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that frames the research question.

claim: Chickadees hide food in concealed, scattered locations and retrieve their caches later in time.
source: Chickadees hide food in concealed, scattered locations and retrieve their caches later in time.
evidence: This is established knowledge about chickadee behavior cited in the abstract.

claim: The apparatus enabled automated tracking of behavioral variables – including caches, retrievals, and investigations of different sites.
source: This apparatus enabled automated tracking of behavioral variables – including caches, retrievals, and investigations of different sites.
evidence: This describes a capability of the experimental apparatus developed in the study.

claim: Chickadees use some navigational strategies that are independent of cache memories, including opportunistic foraging and spatial biases.
source: We found that chickadees use some navigational strategies that are independent of cache memories, including opportunistic foraging and spatial biases.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract based on the modeling results.

claim: Chickadees combine non-mnemonic strategies with spatially precise memories of which sites contain caches and which sites they have previously checked.
source: They combine these strategies with spatially precise memories of which sites contain caches and which sites they have previously checked.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract based on the modeling results.

claim: During caching chickadees avoid sites that contain food, while during retrieval they instead preferentially access occupied sites.
source: A single memory of site contents is used in a context-dependent manner: during caching chickadees avoid sites that contain food, while during retrieval they instead preferentially access occupied sites.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract demonstrating flexible memory use.

claim: The study of episodic memory in animals has been greatly benefitted by experiments that involve spatial navigation.
source: The study of episodic memory in animals has been greatly benefitted by experiments that involve spatial navigation (DeVito and Eichenbaum, 2010; Morris et al., 1982; Salwiczek et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Memory-related neural circuits, like the hippocampus, exhibit well-described firing patterns that correlate to navigational variables – including place and head direction.
source: In addition, memory-related neural circuits, like the hippocampus, exhibit well-described firing patterns that correlate to navigational variables – including place and head direction (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971; Taube et al., 1990).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature on hippocampal place cells and head direction cells.

claim: Navigation is a rich behavior that includes both mnemonic and non-mnemonic spatial strategies.
source: However, navigation is a rich behavior that includes both mnemonic and non-mnemonic spatial strategies.
evidence: This is a general statement about navigation supported by the examples that follow.

claim: An animal using memory to obtain a reward may also engage in opportunistic foraging, use memory-independent search strategies, and exhibit spatial biases.
source: For example, an animal using memory to obtain a reward may also engage in opportunistic foraging, use memory-independent search strategies, and exhibit spatial biases (Dally et al., 2006; Kamil and Roitblat, 1985; Krebs et al., 1974; Lamprea et al., 2008; Pravosudov, 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Food-caching birds hide food in many distinct, concealed locations throughout their environment and later retrieve their caches.
source: These birds hide food in many distinct, concealed locations throughout their environment and later retrieve their caches.
evidence: This is established knowledge about food-caching bird behavior.

claim: In some experiments, spatial navigation is minimized, and birds choose from a small number of available options to obtain food.
source: In some experiments, spatial navigation is minimized, and birds choose from a small number of available options to obtain food (Brodbeck et al., 1992; Clayton and Dickinson, 1998; Clayton and Krebs, 1994a; Salwiczek et al., 2010).
evidence: This describes a type of experimental design used in prior studies, supported by citations.

claim: Tasks with minimal spatial navigation have been ideal for characterizing various contributions to memory, including location, content, and even the relative time of different caches.
source: These tasks have been ideal for characterizing various contributions to memory, including location, content, and even the relative time of different caches.
evidence: This describes the utility of certain experimental designs based on prior literature.

claim: Other experiments have been performed in the wild or in large, naturalistic settings.
source: In contrast, other experiments have been performed in the wild or in large, naturalistic settings (Cowie et al., 1981; Herz et al., 1994; Krushinskaya, 1966; Sherry, 1984a; Stevens and Krebs, 2008).
evidence: This describes another type of experimental design used in prior studies, supported by citations.

claim: Studies in naturalistic settings have been well-suited for measuring spatial properties of the food-caching behavior, including the distribution of caches, large-scale biases, and the spatial specificity of cache memories.
source: These studies have been well-suited for measuring spatial properties of the food-caching behavior, including the distribution of caches, large-scale biases, and the spatial specificity of cache memories.
evidence: This describes the utility of naturalistic experimental designs based on prior literature.

claim: It is unknown how mnemonic and other spatial strategies are coordinated by the animal within a single behavior.
source: However, it is unknown how mnemonic and other spatial strategies are coordinated by the animal within a single behavior.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that motivates the current study.

claim: The experimental setup was developed for a food-caching species, the black-capped chickadee.
source: We developed an experimental setup to fulfill these requirements for a food-caching species, the black-capped chickadee.
evidence: This describes the species used in the study.

claim: Sixty-four cache sites were arranged in an 8 × 8 grid inside a 61 × 61 cm square arena.
source: Sixty-four cache sites were arranged in an 8 × 8 grid inside a 61 × 61 cm square arena.
evidence: This describes the physical layout of the experimental apparatus.

claim: The arena contained a food source in each of the quadrants: a feeder with a motorized cover that could be individually opened or closed.
source: In addition, the arena contained a food source in each of the quadrants: a feeder with a motorized cover that could be individually opened or closed.
evidence: This describes a feature of the experimental apparatus.

claim: The setup allowed navigation on a similar spatial scale to that typically studied in rodents.
source: This setup allowed navigation on a similar spatial scale to that typically studied in rodents (Poucet et al., 2003) while also offering birds a large number of concealed cache sites.
evidence: This compares the spatial scale of the current setup to rodent studies, supported by a citation.

claim: Flaps ensured that no visually guided, memory-independent strategy could be used by the chickadee to determine site contents.
source: Flaps ensured that no visually guided, memory-independent strategy could be used by the chickadee to determine site contents.
evidence: This describes a design feature of the apparatus and its purpose.

claim: Caches, retrievals, and checks could all be detected in the behavior using a single-camera video recording.
source: Thus, caches, retrievals, and checks could all be detected in the behavior using a single-camera video recording.
evidence: This describes a capability of the automated tracking system.

claim: In the Caching task, chickadees were free to cache without any imposed trial structure for 1 hr.
source: In the Caching task (Figure 1E, Figure 1—video 1), chickadees were free to cache without any imposed trial structure for 1 hr.
evidence: This describes the structure of the Caching task.

claim: The Caching task was performed by 17 chickadees.
source: This task was performed by 17 chickadees.
evidence: This reports the number of subjects in the Caching task.

claim: In 10 of the 17 chickadees, enough caches (> 64) were recorded for inclusion in the remainder of the Results section.
source: In 10 of these, we recorded enough caches (> 64; see Materials and methods) for inclusion in the remainder of the Results section.
evidence: This reports the number of subjects included in the analysis and the inclusion criterion.

claim: In the Retrieval task, a trial structure was imposed.
source: In the Retrieval task (Figure 1F, Figure 1—video 2), a trial structure was imposed.
evidence: This describes a feature of the Retrieval task.

claim: In the Retrieval task, once the bird cached 1–3 seeds, lights were turned off for a 2 min delay phase.
source: Once the bird cached 1–3 seeds, lights were turned off for a 2 min delay phase.
evidence: This describes the structure of the Retrieval task.

claim: The Retrieval task was performed by seven chickadees, all of which are included in the analyses.
source: This task was performed by seven chickadees, all of which are included in the analyses.
evidence: This reports the number of subjects in the Retrieval task.

claim: Birds used most of the arena for caching (between 41–64 sites for each of the 10 birds).
source: Birds used most of the arena for caching (between 41–64 sites for each of the 10 birds), but in many cases cache distributions appeared non-uniform.
evidence: This reports a quantitative result about the spatial distribution of caches.

claim: In all birds, entropy was lower than expected by chance (p < 0.001).
source: In all birds, entropy was lower than expected by chance (p < 0.001).
evidence: This reports a statistical result comparing observed entropy to chance.

claim: Birds exhibited spatial biases, even though they cached widely throughout the arena.
source: Therefore, birds exhibited spatial biases, even though they cached widely throughout the arena.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the entropy analysis.

claim: Birds formed two clusters that were well-separated along the first principal component.
source: Remarkably, birds formed two clusters that were well-separated along the first principal component (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This reports a result from principal component analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: The first principal component resembled a bump in the center of the arena, and accounted for 59% of the variance across individuals.
source: The first principal component resembled a bump in the center of the arena (Figure 2C), and accounted for 59% of the variance across individuals (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This reports results from principal component analysis, with reference to figures.

claim: There were two groups of birds: those that preferred to cache in the center of the arena, and those that preferred the edges.
source: Thus, there were two groups of birds: those that preferred to cache in the center of the arena, and those that preferred the edges.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the principal component analysis.

claim: Within-bird correlation values were significantly higher than across-bird correlation values (p < 0.001).
source: Within-bird correlation values were significantly higher than across-bird correlation values (p < 0.001, Figure 2D), even when birds were paired exclusively with birds from the same group (center-preferring or edge-preferring).
evidence: This reports a statistical result comparing within-bird and across-bird correlations.

claim: Birds exhibited individual-specific biases that could not be entirely explained by common biases across a group of birds.
source: Therefore, birds exhibited individual-specific biases that could not be entirely explained by common biases across a group of birds.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation analysis.

claim: The slope of the relationship between lag and correlation was not significantly different from zero (p = 0.49, Bootstrap test).
source: The slope of the relationship between lag and correlation was not significantly different from zero (p = 0.49, Bootstrap test), indicating that there was no detectable drift in bias.
evidence: This reports a statistical result about the stability of biases over time.

claim: There was no detectable drift in bias over time.
source: The slope of the relationship between lag and correlation was not significantly different from zero (p = 0.49, Bootstrap test), indicating that there was no detectable drift in bias.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the regression analysis.

claim: Chickadees exhibit idiosyncratic but stable biases, both in the sites that they check and those that they choose for caching.
source: Collectively, our results suggest that chickadees exhibit idiosyncratic but stable biases, both in the sites that they check and those that they choose for caching.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the spatial bias analyses.

claim: Model #1 performed significantly better than Model #0.
source: We found that this model performed significantly better than Model #0 (see Table 1 for statistics of all model comparisons).
evidence: This reports a result from model comparison, with reference to a table.

claim: The best-fit value of γprv was positive in all birds (0.94 ± 0.21).
source: The best-fit value of γprv was positive in all birds (0.94 ± 0.21), and the best-fit value of σprv was 15.5 ± 0.9 cm (see Table 2 for statistics of all model parameters).
evidence: This reports quantitative results from model fitting.

claim: The best-fit value of σprv was 15.5 ± 0.9 cm.
source: The best-fit value of γprv was positive in all birds (0.94 ± 0.21), and the best-fit value of σprv was 15.5 ± 0.9 cm (see Table 2 for statistics of all model parameters).
evidence: This reports quantitative results from model fitting.

claim: There was roughly a 10-fold increase in probability of caching next to the previous site.
source: Thus, there was roughly a 10-fold (i.e., 100.94) increase in probability of caching next to the previous site, and the spatial extent of this effect was about 1/4 of the arena.
evidence: This interprets the model parameter γprv in terms of probability.

claim: The spatial extent of the proximity effect was about 1/4 of the arena.
source: Thus, there was roughly a 10-fold (i.e., 100.94) increase in probability of caching next to the previous site, and the spatial extent of this effect was about 1/4 of the arena.
evidence: This interprets the model parameter σprv in terms of arena size.

claim: Birds cached closer to previous sites than expected by chance given each bird's spatial bias.
source: To verify this result independently of the model, we compared the observed and expected distances of caches to previous sites and indeed found that birds cached closer to previous sites than expected by chance given each bird's spatial bias (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This reports a result from an independent analysis verifying the model result.

claim: In the Retrieval task, Model #1 performed better than Model #0.
source: We applied the same model to site checks in the Retrieval task. Again, Model #1 performed better than Model #0.
evidence: This reports a result from model comparison in the Retrieval task.

claim: In the Retrieval task, the value of γprv was positive in all birds (1.83 ± 0.42).
source: The value of γprv was positive in all birds (1.83 ± 0.42), indicating a tendency to check sites close to the previous sites, and σprv was 12.9 ± 1.7 cm.
evidence: This reports quantitative results from model fitting in the Retrieval task.

claim: In the Retrieval task, σprv was 12.9 ± 1.7 cm.
source: The value of γprv was positive in all birds (1.83 ± 0.42), indicating a tendency to check sites close to the previous sites, and σprv was 12.9 ± 1.7 cm.
evidence: This reports quantitative results from model fitting in the Retrieval task.

claim: The value of γprv was significantly higher in the Retrieval task (p < 0.05, unpaired t-test).
source: In fact, the value of γprv was significantly higher in the Retrieval task (p < 0.05, unpaired t-test), but the best-fit σprv was not significantly different between the two tasks (p = 0.54, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This reports a statistical comparison between tasks.

claim: The best-fit σprv was not significantly different between the two tasks (p = 0.54, unpaired t-test).
source: In fact, the value of γprv was significantly higher in the Retrieval task (p < 0.05, unpaired t-test), but the best-fit σprv was not significantly different between the two tasks (p = 0.54, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This reports a statistical comparison between tasks.

claim: Birds are influenced by proximity during retrieval more than during caching, even though the spatial extent of this effect is similar during the two behaviors.
source: These results show that birds are influenced by proximity during retrieval more than during caching, even though the spatial extent of this effect is similar during the two behaviors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing model parameters between tasks.

claim: Model #2 performed even better than Model #1.
source: Model #2 performed even better than Model #1, indicating that occupied sites indeed affected the behavior.
evidence: This reports a result from model comparison.

claim: Occupied sites affected the behavior in the Caching task.
source: Model #2 performed even better than Model #1, indicating that occupied sites indeed affected the behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model comparison.

claim: Model #3 performed better than Model #2.
source: We then fit Model #3, in which γemp was additionally introduced as a fourth free parameter to model the effect of checked-empty sites. Model #3 performed better yet, indicating that checked-empty sites also affected the behavior.
evidence: This reports a result from model comparison.

claim: Checked-empty sites affected the behavior in the Caching task.
source: We then fit Model #3, in which γemp was additionally introduced as a fourth free parameter to model the effect of checked-empty sites. Model #3 performed better yet, indicating that checked-empty sites also affected the behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model comparison.

claim: Across birds, the value of γocc was negative (–0.32 ± 0.17).
source: Across birds, the value of γocc was negative (–0.32 ± 0.17), whereas the value of γemp was positive (0.13 ± 0.05).
evidence: This reports quantitative results from model fitting.

claim: Across birds, the value of γemp was positive (0.13 ± 0.05).
source: Across birds, the value of γocc was negative (–0.32 ± 0.17), whereas the value of γemp was positive (0.13 ± 0.05).
evidence: This reports quantitative results from model fitting.

claim: There was roughly a twofold decrease in probability of caching into occupied sites.
source: These values indicate roughly a twofold decrease in probability of caching into occupied sites and a 1.3-fold increase in probability of caching into checked-empty sites.
evidence: This interprets the model parameter γocc in terms of probability.

claim: There was a 1.3-fold increase in probability of caching into checked-empty sites.
source: These values indicate roughly a twofold decrease in probability of caching into occupied sites and a 1.3-fold increase in probability of caching into checked-empty sites.
evidence: This interprets the model parameter γemp in terms of probability.

claim: Both results are consistent with chickadees spreading their caches throughout the arena, rather than pooling them into the same sites.
source: Both results are consistent with chickadees spreading their caches throughout the arena, rather than pooling them into the same sites.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model results.

claim: Chickadees tended to cache into occupied sites less often than expected by chance.
source: Indeed, chickadees tended to cache into occupied sites less often than expected by chance (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This reports a result from an independent analysis verifying the model result.

claim: In the Retrieval task, introducing γocc and γemp significantly improved the fit of the model.
source: We again applied the same models to site checks in the Retrieval task (Figure 5C–D). As in the Caching task, introducing γocc and γemp significantly improved the fit of the model.
evidence: This reports a result from model comparison in the Retrieval task.

claim: In the Retrieval task, the signs of the two parameters were reversed compared to the Caching task: γocc was positive in all birds (0.26 ± 0.09), whereas γemp was negative in all birds (–0.14 ± 0.07).
source: However, the signs of the two parameters were reversed compared to the Caching task: γocc was positive in all birds (0.26 ± 0.09), whereas γemp was negative in all birds (–0.14 ± 0.07).
evidence: This reports quantitative results from model fitting in the Retrieval task.

claim: Birds were attracted to occupied sites during the feeder-closed phase of the Retrieval task.
source: These results show that birds were attracted to occupied sites during the feeder-closed phase of the task.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model results.

claim: Birds being attracted to occupied sites during retrieval is consistent with chickadees searching for their caches.
source: This is consistent with chickadees searching for their caches.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model results.

claim: Chickadees found their caches after fewer checks than expected by chance: 8.5 ± 5.6 checks in the observed data, compared to 20.8 ± 4.5 checks in data where trajectories were shuffled between trials.
source: Indeed, chickadees found their caches after fewer checks than expected by chance: 8.5 ± 5.6 checks in the observed data, compared to 20.8 ± 4.5 checks in data where trajectories were shuffled between trials (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This reports a result from an independent analysis verifying the model result.

claim: Neither Model #4 nor Model #5 was an improvement over Model #3.
source: We introduced either σocc or σemp as an additional free parameter (Model #4 and Model #5 respectively, Figure 5E–H). Neither model was an improvement over Model #3.
evidence: This reports a result from model comparison.

claim: The best-fit values of σocc and σemp in both models were between 0.01 and 0.02 cm, much smaller than the distance between neighboring sites (7.1 cm).
source: In fact, the best-fit values of σocc and σemp in both models were between 0.01 and 0.02 cm, much smaller than the distance between neighboring sites (7.1 cm).
evidence: This reports quantitative results from model fitting.

claim: The effects of site contents on chickadee behavior were site-specific, and were small even at neighboring sites of the arena.
source: Thus, the effects of site contents on chickadee behavior were site-specific, and were small even at neighboring sites of the arena.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model results.

claim: This site specificity is consistent with that demonstrated under different conditions by previous work.
source: This site specificity is consistent with that demonstrated under different conditions by previous work (Cowie et al., 1981).
evidence: This compares the current result to prior literature.

claim: After obtaining a seed, a chickadee may simply check multiple sites in the arena and preferentially cache into an empty one that it encounters, which would be a visually-guided strategy that does not require memory.
source: However, after obtaining a seed, a chickadee may simply check multiple sites in the arena and preferentially cache into an empty one that it encounters. This would be a visually-guided strategy that does not require memory.
evidence: This describes an alternative explanation for the observed behavior.

claim: Chickadees usually cached into the first site that they opened after visiting the food source (79% of caches).
source: We considered this possibility unlikely because chickadees usually cached into the first site that they opened after visiting the food source (79% of caches).

claim: When fitting models to first checks, γocc in Model #2 was still significantly negative, and γemp in Model #3 was still significantly positive.
source: We found that γocc in Model #2 was still significantly negative, and γemp in Model #3 was still significantly positive (Figure 6A–B).

claim: Chickadees did not merely check sites until finding an empty one, but actually used memories of which sites were occupied and which were empty.
source: Therefore, chickadees did not merely check sites until finding an empty one. Rather, they actually used memories of which sites were occupied and which were empty.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the first check analysis.

claim: When fitting Model #2 to first checks in the Retrieval task, γocc was still positive.
source: We also fit Model #2 to first checks in the Retrieval task. In this case, γocc was still positive.
evidence: This reports a result from model fitting to first checks in the Retrieval task.

claim: Chickadees had an increased probability of checking an occupied site even on the first attempt, implying that chickadees did not search the arena until finding a cache, but used memories of occupied sites.
source: In other words, chickadees had an increased probability of checking an occupied site even on the first attempt. This implies that chickadees did not search the arena until finding a cache, but used memories of occupied sites.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the first check analysis in the Retrieval task.

claim: Chickadees are not known to use olfaction for finding food.
source: Chickadees are not known to use olfaction for finding food (Cowie et al., 1981; Herz et al., 1994; Sherry, 1984a), and previous studies have excluded this possibility by removing caches during the delay period of the task.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Even when caches were removed from the arena, chickadees tended to spend more time at the locations of the missing caches after a delay period of up to 1 hr.
source: Consistent with published results, even when caches were removed from the arena, chickadees tended to spend more time at the locations of the missing caches after a delay period of up to 1 hr (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This reports a result from the olfactory control experiment.

claim: Chickadees have memories of site contents.
source: Collectively, our results show that chickadees have memories of site contents, as in previous work (Clayton and Dickinson, 1999; Sherry, 1984a).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analyses, consistent with prior literature.

claim: Chickadees use memories of site contents in flexible ways, both during caching and during retrieval.
source: They use these memory of site contents in flexible ways, both during caching and during retrieval.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analyses showing context-dependent use of memory.

claim: In the Retrieval task, chickadees often 'recached' seeds after retrieving them (44% of all retrievals).
source: In the feeder-closed phase of the Retrieval task, chickadees often 'recached' seeds after retrieving them (44% of all retrievals).

claim: Model #6 fit the data significantly better than Model #1, and Model #7 fit the data even better than Model #6.
source: We found that Model #6 fit the data significantly better than Model #1, and Model #7 fit the data even better than Model #6 (Figure 6D).

claim: Birds were attracted to all of their caches during retrieval, but had a stronger preference for the recent recaches.
source: These results indicate that birds were attracted to all of their caches during retrieval, but had a stronger preference for the recent recaches.

claim: Neither Model #8 nor Model #9 improved the fit to the data.

source: The best-fit values of τocc and τemp were very large (both >44 min, Figure 6G).

claim: There did not appear to be a significant memory decay at the timescale of our experiments.
source: Therefore, there did not appear to be a significant memory decay at the timescale of our experiments.

claim: The preference for retrieving recaches may be a behavioral preference unrelated to a memory decay.
source: This additionally implies that the preference for retrieving recaches may be a behavioral preference unrelated to a memory decay.

claim: Chickadees often recheck sites, with a median of 2.4 min between consecutive checks of the same site.
source: Chickadees often recheck sites, with a median of 2.4 min between consecutive checks of the same site.

claim: Prior work has showed some memories lasting up to a month, even when birds are not allowed to recheck their sites.
source: However, prior work has showed some memories lasting up to a month, even when birds are not allowed to recheck their sites (Roth et al., 2012).

claim: Memory did not appear to decay at capacities tested by our experiments.
source: Therefore, memory did not appear to decay at capacities tested by our experiments.

claim: Several natural features of chickadee spatial navigation were preserved in this environment.

claim: Chickadees rely on multiple strategies for caching and retrieval and use memory in flexible ways during these behaviors.
